rows.speaker: أبو أمامة الباهلي
rows.claim: A report attributed to Abu Umama and raised to the Prophet tells of Thalaba's repeated request for wealth, broken charity pledge, neglect of communal worship, and refusal to pay, after which the Prophet lamented him.
rows.anchor: عن أبي أمامة الباهلي وروي ذلك مرفوعا

rows.speaker: ابن عباس وسعيد بن جبير وقتادة
rows.claim: They report that Thalaba pledged before a group of Ansar to give charity and support kin if enriched; after inheriting from a cousin, he failed to fulfill the pledge.
rows.anchor: عن ابن عباس وسعيد بن جبير وقتادة

rows.speaker: الحسن ومجاهد
rows.claim: They identify Thalaba ibn Hatib and Muattib ibn Qushayr of Banu Amr ibn Awf as the two men who vowed charity when granted wealth, then became miserly.
rows.anchor: فلما رزقهما الله المال بخلا به عن الحسن ومجاهد

rows.speaker: الضحاك
rows.claim: Al-Dahhak says the verses concern hypocrites Natl ibn al-Harith, Jad ibn Qays, Thalaba ibn Hatib, and Muattib ibn Qushayr.
rows.anchor: وثعلبة بن حاطب ومعتب بن قشير عن الضحاك

rows.speaker: الكلبي
rows.claim: Al-Kalbi identifies Hatib ibn Abi Baltaa, whose money in Syria was delayed; he vowed charity if it arrived, but did not do so when it came.
rows.anchor: فآتاه الله تعالى ذلك فلم يفعل عن الكلبي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Some of them” refers to the hypocrites mentioned earlier, who pledged that if God gave them provision they would give charity and become righteous through spending, kinship, and helping the needy.
rows.anchor: أي من جملة المنافقين الذين تقدم ذكرهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: When God granted the wealth they desired, they withheld it and its due from God, turned away from His command, and were averse to His religion.
rows.anchor: عن الوفاء بالعهد ومنعوا حق الله منه

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Hasan explains that their miserliness caused hypocrisy to take root in their hearts, like saying a person's association with someone caused him to abandon learning.
rows.anchor: عن الحسن كأنهم حصلوا على النفاق بسبب البخل

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujahid reads the consequence as God depriving them of repentance, as with Iblis; their inability to repent is inferred from the reported outcome.
rows.anchor: حرمان التوبة كما حرم إبليس عن مجاهد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One explanation takes “the day they meet Him” as the day they meet the recompense for miserliness, with the offense named in place of its recompense.
rows.anchor: فذكر البخل وأراد به جزاءه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The question rebukes the hypocrites and means that they ought to know God is aware of what they conceal and privately discuss.
rows.anchor: أي ألم يعلم هؤلاء المنافقون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Their secret” is what they hide within themselves, and “their private conversation” is what they say confidentially among themselves.
rows.anchor: أي ما يخفون في أنفسهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The plural “unseen things” covers what is absent from bodies and human perception, whether existent or nonexistent, in every respect it can be known; the form is intensive.
rows.anchor: جمع غيب وهو كل ما غاب عن الأجسام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One sin can lead to another: neglect of this due led them to persist in hypocrisy until death; acts of obedience likewise lead to more obedience, as religious duties are ordered.
rows.anchor: دلالة على أن بعض المعاصي قد يدعو إلى بعض

rows.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: The Prophet states that a hypocrite has three signs: he lies when speaking, breaks promises, and betrays a trust; al-Tabrisi says the report is sound.
rows.anchor: صح في الحديث عن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their punishment followed their evil conduct: they broke their promise to God and lied.
rows.anchor: بين سبحانه أن هذا إنما أصابهم بفعلهم السيئ

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternatively, “the day they meet Him” is the day they meet God, when no one but God controls benefit or harm; the verse predicts they will die hypocrites, a report fulfilled as stated.
rows.anchor: معناه إلى يوم يلقون الله

rows.speaker: أهل الكوفة غير أبي بكر
rows.claim: The Kufan readers except Abu Bakr read “inna salataka” in the singular, as in Hud; the remaining readers use the plural “salawatuka.”
rows.anchor: قرأ أهل الكوفة غير أبي بكر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Prayer in Arabic means supplication; al-A'sha's verse uses the verb for a prayer over a wine jar, supporting the command to supplicate for the donors.
rows.anchor: الصلاة في اللغة الدعاء قال الأعشى

rows.speaker: سيبويه
rows.claim: Sibawayh treats phrases such as God’s prayer on His messenger and “woe to the defrauders” as descriptions of those deserving the expression, not prayers from God; he applies the same account to related forms.
rows.anchor: وهذا مذهب سيبويه فإذا كانت الصلاة مصدرا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: As a verbal noun, “salat” has the same form for singular and plural, like “voice”; when kinds differ it may take a plural, as in the verse about the lowest of voices.
rows.anchor: فإذا كانت الصلاة مصدرا وقع على الجمع والمفرد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Tabrisi rejects the claim that singular salat is for many and plural salawat for few: the feminine plural can denote either, as in the cited verses.
rows.anchor: فأما من زعم أن الصلاة أولى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Tutahhiruhum” may modify “charity,” with its feminine subject and “bihā” explanatory; or address the Prophet—“you purify them by it”—with the clause still modifying charity.
rows.anchor: إما أن يكون صفة لصدقة ويكون التاء للتأنيث

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Unlike “tutahhiruhum,” “tuzakkīhim” can only address the Prophet directly.
rows.anchor: وأما { وتزكيهم } فلا يكون إلا للخطاب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Although “tutahhiruhum” could begin an independent clause, al-Tabrisi prefers connecting it syntactically to what precedes.
rows.anchor: يجوز أن يكون على الاستئناف وحمله على الاتصال أولى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Min” is partitive, since not all wealth must be given; “their wealth” rather than “their property” includes all kinds of assets, generally requiring collection across Muslims’ wealth except where evidence excludes a category.
rows.anchor: أدخل من للتبعيض لأنه لم يجب

rows.speaker: الحسن وغيره
rows.claim: One view takes the command as a special, intensified penitential charity from these repentant people, not the obligatory zakat.
rows.anchor: الكفارة للذنوب التي أصابوها عن الحسن وغيره

rows.speaker: الجبائي وأكثر أهل التفسير
rows.claim: Al-Jubba'i and most exegetes identify the charity as obligatory zakat, which al-Tabrisi calls the apparent reading absent evidence for restriction; he lists the nisab thresholds for silver, gold, livestock, crops, and fruit.
rows.anchor: عن الجبائي وأكثر أهل التفسير

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The charity cleanses them of sin, while the Prophet attributes purity to them and prays for their purification; alternatively, both verbs describe what the Prophet does through the charity.
rows.anchor: تلك الصدقة عن دنس الذنوب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God commands the Prophet to pray that those giving charity have it accepted, using a supplication asking God to reward their gift and bless what remains.
rows.anchor: هذا أمر من الله تعالى للنبي صلى الله عليه وسلم

rows.speaker: عبد الله بن أبي أوفى
rows.claim: The Prophet used to pray for groups bringing charity; Abdullah ibn Abi Awfa brought charity and heard him pray for his family. Al-Bukhari and Muslim include the report in their Sahih collections.
rows.anchor: فأتاه ابن أبي أوفى بصدقة فقال اللهم صل على آل أبي أوفى أورده البخاري ومسلم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Sakan” means that the Prophet’s supplications quiet the donors’ souls.
rows.anchor: أي إن دعواتك مما تسكن نفوسهم إليه

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas explains “sakan” as mercy for the donors.
rows.anchor: رحمة لهم عن ابن عباس

rows.speaker: قتادة والكلبي
rows.claim: Qatada and al-Kalbi understand it as assurance and tranquility that God has accepted their charity.
rows.anchor: وقار وطمأنينة لهم أن الله قد قبل منهم عن قتادة والكلبي

rows.speaker: أبو عبيدة
rows.claim: Abu Ubayda glosses “sakan” as support or confirmation for them.
rows.anchor: تثبيت لهم عن أبي عبيدة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God hears the Prophet’s prayer for them and knows how they handle charity.
rows.anchor: يسمع دعاءك لهم ويعلم ما يكون منهم في الصدقات

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The question prompts the hearer to recognize that God accepts repentance; knowing this motivates hastening to repentance and brings reward and escape from punishment.
rows.anchor: استفهام يراد به التنبيه على ما يجب أن يعلم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The repentant had asked the Prophet to take their wealth as expiation; he waited for divine permission, and God clarifies that acceptance belongs to God, not the Prophet.
rows.anchor: لما سألوا النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم أن يأخذ من أموالهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God’s taking the charities means accepting them and guaranteeing their reward.
rows.anchor: أي يتقبلها ويضمن الجزاء عليها

rows.speaker: الجبائي
rows.claim: Al-Jubba'i says God calls the Prophet’s and believers’ collection of charity His own taking by metaphor, because they act on His command.
rows.anchor: جعل الله أخذ النبي والمؤمنين للصدقات أخذا من الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The root of “fatara” means to split, as a leaf splits from a tree; God's creating beings is likened to their emerging from that split, with Adam created from earth.
rows.anchor: الفطر الشق عن أمر الله كما ينفطر الورق عن الشجر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Midrar” is abundant, continuous rain in the needed measure but not harmful excess; its “mif'al” pattern intensifies, like “mi'tar” and “miqdim.”
rows.anchor: المدرار الدار الكثير المتتابع على قدر الحاجة إليه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “I'tarāka” derives from “ʿarāhu yaʿrūhu,” meaning that something struck or afflicted him; a poet’s cited line illustrates the usage.
rows.anchor: واعتراك من قولهم عراه يعروه إذا أصابه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Inẓār” means granting someone respite to consider his affairs; “ta'khīr” simply means putting something later rather than earlier.
rows.anchor: والفرق بين الإنظار والتأخير أن الإنظار إمهال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The “nāṣiya” is the forelock; its root connotes connection, as in a desert joining another desert, with cited verse fragments using the root.
rows.anchor: والناصية قصاص الشعر وأصله الاتصال

rows.speaker: أبو النجم
rows.claim: Abu al-Najm's verse about gray hairs and “al-manāṣī” is cited as evidence for the root's sense of joining or pulling something together.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو النجم: إن يمس رأسي أشمط العناصي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Al-ʿanīd” means a defiant tyrant; the related verb can mean acting arrogantly or turning away from a matter.
rows.anchor: العنيد العاتي الطاغي عند يعند عنودا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Akhāhum” is accusative after an implied “We sent”; Hud is an apposition, and “ʿĀd” may be declinable as a people name but indeclinable as a tribe name.
rows.anchor: نصب بتقدير أرسلنا كأنه قال وأرسلنا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: For “ghayruhu,” the nominative reading follows syntactic position, while the genitive follows the word's surface form.
rows.anchor: من ضم الراء حمل الصفة على الموضع

rows.speaker: صاحب كتاب كشف الجامع النحوي
rows.claim: The grammarian treats “in” as a negative particle: the people deny saying anything except the claim that an idol afflicted Hud; the exception is from the verbal noun implied by “say,” as in the cited verses.
rows.anchor: قال صاحب كتاب كشف الجامع النحوي إن حرف لحقت نفي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The order to seek forgiveness before repentance was explained earlier in this sura.
rows.anchor: قد بينا وجه تقديم الاستغفار على التوبة في أول هذه السورة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The promise means that God sends abundant, successive rain; since the people were in drought, repentance would bring fertile land, growth, fruit, and life-giving water.
rows.anchor: أي يرسل المطر عليكم متتابعا متواترا دارا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The promised provision is compared with God making an opening and providing from an unexpected source for the God-fearing.
rows.anchor: ومن يتق الله يجعل له مخرجا ويرزقه من حيث لا يحتسب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Strength” is explained as wealth, children, or physical might—anything a person draws strength from.
rows.anchor: فسرت القوة هنا بالمال والولد والشدة

rows.speaker: علي بن عيسى
rows.claim: Ali ibn Isa interprets the promise as added honor through greater numbers and wealth.
rows.anchor: علي بن عيسى: يريد عزا إلى عزكم بكثرة عددكم وأموالكم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another explanation is an increase in faith in addition to bodily strength.
rows.anchor: قوة في إيمانكم إلى قوة أبدانكم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The people say Hud brought no clear proof or miracle that would establish his truthfulness.
rows.anchor: أي بحجة ومعجزة تبين صدقك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One grammatical explanation makes “ʿan” stand in place of “bāʾ,” so the meaning is “because of your statement.”
rows.anchor: إن عن جعلت مكان الباء فمعناه بقولك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: They reject the proof because they imitate ancestors and leaders, dismiss its bearer without examining the evidence, doubt its validity, and hold false premises leading them to deny it.
rows.anchor: أشياء منها تقليد الآباء والرؤساء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: They worship idols because they think these bring them near God, Satan promises worldly favor through them, or anthropomorphist ideas lead them to make idols in the imagined divine form.
rows.anchor: أشياء منها اعتقادهم أن عبادتها تقربهم إلى الله زلفى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their declaration means that they do not believe or affirm Hud's message.
rows.anchor: أي مصدقين وإنما حملهم على دفع البينة

words: إِن نَّقُولُ إِلَّا ٱعْتَرَىٰكَ بَعْضُ ءَالِهَتِنَا بِسُوٓءٍ
rows.speaker: ابن عباس ومجاهد
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas and Mujahid explain the accusation as the people claiming an idol made Hud insane because he insulted and reviled it.
rows.anchor: ذهب إليه ابن عباس ومجاهد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Hud calls God to witness and then calls the people to witness his disavowal of their associates, challenging their claim that the idols harmed him.
rows.anchor: أي وأشهدكم أيضا بعد إشهاد الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He addresses even disbelieving, corrupt people to establish proof against them, not because their testimony is needed; his declaration is warning and excuse.
rows.anchor: إقامة للحجة عليهم لا لتقوم الحجة بهم

rows.speaker: سيبويه
rows.claim: Sibawayh treats “mithla mā” in the cited verse as nominative and adjective-like, opened because it is annexed to “mā”; Abu Uthman instead makes the two words one noun built on fatḥ, though the line does not decide the issue.
rows.anchor: مثل في موضع رفع في قول سيبويه وقد جرى وصفا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The kasra in “idh” marks the meeting of two vowelless sounds after its annexed clause is omitted; tanwin signals the omitted complement.
rows.anchor: فأما الكسرة في إذ فلالتقاء الساكنين

rows.speaker: سيبويه
rows.claim: Sibawayh distinguishes names used for a people, tribe, or ancestor, and names whose use is evenly shared; Thamud and Saba belong to the last type.
rows.anchor: هو ثمود وسبأ فهما مرة للقبيلتين ومرة للحيين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Because Thamud equally denotes tribe and people, either declension or non-declension is acceptable, as is varying by position; al-Tabrisi says recitation must follow the transmitted readers.
rows.anchor: فمن صرف في جميع المواضع كان حسنا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse “a people of Taghlib” combines “people” with “daughter of Wa'il,” illustrating that a name can be used for both a community and its tribe.
rows.anchor: كسا الله حي تغلب ابنة وائل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Poetry and a hadith show “Yahud” as a tribe name and therefore uninflected; the same argument applies to “Majus,” which would be inflected if it named a people.
rows.anchor: فقد قامت الدلالة على أن يهود استعملت على أنها للقبيلة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Inshāʾ” means originating something without using other means; the related form “anshaʾa” also begins a story or poem.
rows.anchor: إيجاد ابتداء من غير استعانة بشيء من الأسباب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Istiʿmār” means enabling someone capable to cultivate the earth; “ʿumrā” is a legal gift of a house for a lifetime.
rows.anchor: والاستعمار جعل القادر يعمر الأرض كعمارة الدار

rows.speaker: علي بن عيسى
rows.claim: Ali ibn Isa distinguishes “mass,” which can occur between inanimate things, from “lams,” which requires two living beings because it involves perception.
rows.anchor: وفرق علي بن عيسى بينهما

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Juthum” is glossed either as falling face-down or as sitting on one's knee.
rows.anchor: والجثوم السقوط على الوجه. وقيل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Ghaniya bi-l-makān” means to reside there and “al-maghnā” is a dwelling; al-Nabigha's line illustrates it. The root also denotes sufficiency, wealth, or song as a self-sufficient sound.
rows.anchor: وغني بالمكان إذا أقام به والمغنى المنزل قال النابغة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Araʾaytum” has no direct object because it is suspended over a self-standing clause; the first conditional takes “fa” as its answer, while the second answer is omitted and understood as who will protect me if I disobey.
rows.anchor: لا مفعول له ههنا لأنه معلق كما يعلق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Although “man yansuruni” is phrased as a question, it means there would be no protector from God if صالح disobeyed; “araʾaytum” may be ignored because the clause stands independently.
rows.anchor: ومن ينصرني صورته صورة الاستفهام ومعناه النفي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Fa-yākhudhukum” is subjunctive as the consequence of a prohibition: if they touch the camel harmfully, an immediate punishment will seize them.
rows.anchor: جواب النهي بالفاء ولذلك نصبه وتقديره لا يقع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Ayyām” derives from “aywām,” with the waw changed into yāʾ and assimilated into the preceding yāʾ.
rows.anchor: وأيام أصله أيوام قلبت الواو ياء

rows.speaker: الجبائي
rows.claim: Al-Jubba'i locates Thamud in Wadi al-Qura between Medina and Syria and ʿĀd in Yemen.
rows.anchor: وكان ثمود بوادي القرى بين المدينة والشام وكان عاد باليمن عن الجبائي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “He originated you from earth” means God began human creation from earth by creating Adam from it, from whom people descend.
rows.anchor: أي ابتدأ خلقكم من الأرض لأنه خلق آدم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “He settled you in it” means God made people cultivators of the earth, enabled them to develop it, and made them need to live there.
rows.anchor: أي جعلكم عمار الأرض بأن مكنكم من عمارتها

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujahid explains “istʿmarakum” as God granting the earth to people for the duration of their lifetimes.
rows.anchor: مدة إعماركم من العمرى عن مجاهد

rows.speaker: الضحاك
rows.claim: Al-Dahhak reads the phrase as lengthening people's lives on earth, saying their lifespans ranged from one thousand to three hundred years.
rows.anchor: وأطال فيها أعماركم عن الضحاك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A further reading is that God commanded the necessary development of earth through housing, farming, and planting trees; this rebuts the claim that earning a livelihood is forbidden.
rows.anchor: أمركم من عمارتها بما تحتاجون إليه من المساكن والزراعات

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: صالح tells them to seek forgiveness for idolatry and sins, then persist in repentance; God is near in mercy to monotheists and answers those who call on Him.
rows.anchor: فاستغفروه من الشرك والذنوب ثم دوموا على التوبة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The people say they once hoped صالح would do good because of his admirable character, but his present teaching ended that hope; alternatively, they expected him to support their religion.
rows.anchor: أي كنا نرجو منك الخير لما كنت عليه من الأحوال الجميلة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their question about his forbidding ancestral worship is a repudiating challenge, as though it were unthinkable to forbid what their fathers worshipped.
rows.anchor: استفهام معناه الإنكار كأنهم أنكروا أن ينهى الإنسان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their “doubt that causes suspicion” means a doubt that breeds accusation: they assume their forebears were not ignorant or astray.
rows.anchor: موجب للريبة والتهمة إذ لم يكن آباؤنا في جهالة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: صالح says that if God gave him proof and prophethood, no one can shield him from divine punishment should he disobey.
rows.anchor: أي وأعطاني الله منه نعمة وهي النبوة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “You add only loss” means their demand attributes loss to them, not صالح.
rows.anchor: غير نسبتي إياكم إلى الخسارة

rows.speaker: ابن الأعرابي
rows.claim: Ibn al-A'rabi explicitly glosses the loss as theirs, not صالح's.
rows.anchor: ابن الأعرابي: يريد غير تخسير لكم لا لي

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas says their words make صالح more certain that they are lost.
rows.anchor: ابن عباس: ما تزيدونني إلا بصيرة في خسارتكم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another explanation is that complying with their invitation would make صالح someone who increases in loss.
rows.anchor: معناه إن أجبتكم إلى ما تدعونني إليه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The she-camel was God's sign: she emerged from a rock as requested, pregnant, drank all the water on her day, and left the water to other animals on the alternate day.
rows.anchor: أخرجها لهم من جوف صخرة يشاهدونها على تلك الصفة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Āyatan” is a circumstantial accusative describing the camel; she is attributed to God to honor her, as with the House of God.
rows.anchor: وانتصب آية على الحال من ناقة الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Let it eat in God's earth” may be a circumstantial clause describing the camel grazing or an independent sentence; the grazing is grass and plants.
rows.anchor: فاتركوها في حال أكلها فتكون تأكل في أرض الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Do not touch it with harm” means do not strike, kill, wound, or otherwise injure it; doing so would bring immediate punishment.
rows.anchor: بسوء } قتل أو جرح أو غيره

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One person hamstrung the camel and the rest approved; its killer was al-Ahmar of Thamud, whose name became an Arabic proverb for ill fortune.
rows.anchor: عقرها بعضهم ورضي به البعض وإنما عقرها أحمر ثمود

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: صالح tells them to enjoy for three days the pleasant sights, sounds, and other sensory experiences of their land before punishment arrives.
rows.anchor: تلذذوا بما تريدون من المدركات الحسنة من المناظر والأصوات

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A country is called “dār” because it gathers its inhabitants as a house gathers its occupants; “diyār Rabiʿa” and “diyār Mudar” illustrate the usage.
rows.anchor: ويقال للبلاد دار لأنها تجمع أهلها كما تجمع الدار أهلها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another explanation takes “in your dwelling” to mean in the worldly life.
rows.anchor: في داركم يعني دار الدنيا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternatively, the command means “live in your town”; life is described as enjoyment because the living person experiences the senses.
rows.anchor: عيشوا في بلدكم وعبر عن الحياة بالتمتع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A report says that after the camel was hamstrung, its calf climbed a mountain and roared three times; صالح assigned one day to each roar, and the people's faces turned yellow, then red, then black before the promised punishment.
rows.anchor: لما عقرت الناقة صعد فصيلها الجبل ورغا ثلاث مرات

rows.speaker: جابر بن عبد الله الأنصاري
rows.claim: Jabir reports that during the Prophet's Tabuk sermon at al-Hijr, he warned people not to demand signs: صالح's people requested a camel with appointed drinking days, then defied God and received the three-day reprieve before the blast destroyed them. Abu Righal escaped in the sanctuary; the Prophet identified him as Abu Thaqif. No grading is stated.
rows.anchor: وروى جابر بن عبد الله الأنصاري أن رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم
